items.a: An open-source framework for evaluating agents on **real tasks with real data** in **isolated sandboxes**.

items.q: What three parts make up a Harbor task?
items.a: An **instruction** in markdown, an **environment** (a seeded Dockerfile) and **verifiers** that check the result.
A **reward**, often a simple **pass/fail**, written to a file.

items.q: Why does Harbor run several trials of each task?
items.a: Agents are **stochastic**, so each trial gets a **fresh container** and an independent run.

items.q: Why are verifiers mounted only after the agent finishes?
items.a: So the agent **can't read them and cheat**.

items.q: What do canonical verifiers look at?
items.a: Only **what the agent leaves behind**, its side effects, not how it got there.
You can **hold tasks constant** and swap prompts, tools, harnesses or models to see real **improvements or regressions**.

items.q: What is an oracle in Harbor?
items.a: A **known solution script** that checks data, environment and verifiers **before you spend tokens** on an agent.

items.q: How does the Phoenix team test its agents with Harbor?
items.a: It puts the **whole single-node server and a realistic SQLite file** in Docker and verifies via the API or database.

items.q: What did one prompt change show in their experiments?
items.a: The agent **used SQL instead of paginating the API** and made **fewer tool calls**.

items.q: What if your system is too distributed to fit in a container?
items.a: Hide the agent behind a **stable interface** and test that boundary.
